clue.text: Plato's exemplary way to settle accounts?

parts.note: the clue word is what you get when the letters of postal are put in a new order, so the answer read as an instruction builds it

explanation.surface: A philosopher's model method of paying one's bills.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: put POSTAL in ORDER and you get PLATOS, the clue's first word. 'Exemplary' just colours the surface, hinting at Plato's ideal Forms. A postal order was a British money order bought at a post office.
explanation.definitionFit: A postal order is a money order bought at the post office and used for paying bills or debts.

clue.text: Celebrate when new penny's gone without time to have old penny

annotationWithheld.why: Celebrate when new penny's gone without time to have old penny (5,3,4,3): no parse found that builds the answer from the wordplay; no blog for this puzzle
annotationWithheld.clue: Celebrate when new penny's gone without time to have old penny

clue.text: Run-down sound of recorded device

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is spoken, so the letters we want say the device's name out loud

parts.note: a CD is a compact disc, a device holding a recording

explanation.surface: The noise a cassette or disc player makes is shabby.
explanation.definitionFit: Seedy and run-down are synonyms for shabby and squalid, as of a neglected area.

clue.text: Use rate in knots from stern

indicators.note: something tied in knots is tangled, so these letters are twisted into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to a sailor to measure speed in knots from the back of the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knots' and 'stern' set a nautical scene, but 'in knots' signals the anagram of USE RATE, and 'stern' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and stern are synonyms for strict, severe in manner.

clue.text: When Bobby can have rest of rum?

definitions.meaning: a bobby is a British policeman; off his patrol route he is free to relax
rum is old British slang for strange or odd

explanation.surface: A question about when a policeman may enjoy the rest of his rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink; it is the slang adjective for odd. A bobby is a British policeman, whose beat is his patrol route.
explanation.definitionFit: Offbeat means unconventional or odd, the same sense as the British slang 'rum'.

clue.text: Fight at sound of bell

definitions.meaning: British slang for a heated argument or scrap
the two-note chime a bell makes

explanation.definitionFit: Ding-dong is informal British for a noisy fight and also imitates the chime of a bell.

clue.text: "Tainted love" is pretty clever with hindsight

indicators.note: something tainted is spoiled or corrupted, so these letters are turned into a different arrangement

parts.note: love means nil in tennis scoring, shown as the letter O

explanation.surface: A remark looking back on the song Tainted Love and calling it rather clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tainted Love' is a hit song, but 'Tainted' is the anagram signal, and 'love' gives O (zero in tennis), shuffled with IS PRETTY CLEVER.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrospectively means looking back on past events, which is what judging with hindsight does.

clue.text: It's about setter's rising drug problem of old, of course

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the letters built so far are read from bottom to top
about here means going round, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: taken as the letters ITS
the setter refers to himself as me, so his possession is MY
E is the slang abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A golfer's grumble that an old problem on the course involved a drug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts one piece round the other, and 'rising' turns that combination upwards before the drug is added. 'Of course' means on a golf course, where the stymie rule once applied.
explanation.definitionFit: A stymie was a golfing situation, abolished in 1952, where an opponent's ball blocked the line to the hole.

clue.text: Take mushroom restricted by legislation

indicators.note: something restricted by another is held within it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: an Act is a piece of legislation passed by Parliament
a cep is an edible wild mushroom, the porcini

explanation.surface: A command to pick a mushroom whose picking the law limits.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept something is to take what is offered; the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Jiffy note at foot of member's stretcher

indicators.note: a piece at the foot comes after the other, closing the word as a footnote closes a letter

parts.note: a jiffy and a trice both mean an instant
PS is a postscript, a note added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A hurried postscript left at the bottom of a hospital stretcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretcher' suggests a hospital litter; here it is a muscle that straightens a limb, the 'member'.
explanation.definitionFit: The triceps is the muscle that straightens, or extends, the arm, a limb or member of the body.

clue.text: Cool to take an unconscious jerk's anorak

parts.note: to fan something is to cool it with moving air
a tic is an involuntary twitch of a muscle

explanation.surface: Someone using a fan on the coat of a fool who has passed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anorak' looks like the coat; in British slang it is an obsessive enthusiast, a nerd.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak in British slang is an obsessive hobbyist, a single-minded enthusiast or zealot.

clue.text: Radical left the enemy bewildered

indicators.note: someone bewildered is confused, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A political extremist leaves the opposing side baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Radical' reads as a political extremist; in chemistry it is a group of atoms. L (left) is shuffled with THE ENEMY.
explanation.definitionFit: Methylene is a chemical radical, a CH2 group of atoms that acts as a unit in compounds.

clue.text: Motivated by crowd

definitions.meaning: ... as the past tense of drive, to push or impel someone
a large moving mass of people or animals

explanation.definitionFit: Drove is both the past tense of drive, to impel, and a noun for a herd or throng.

clue.text: Nymph with one choice that's not on ice

indicators.note: the letters of the last two words are what is not wanted, so they are struck out of the pool and the rest rearranged

parts.note: taken as written into the letter pool; the run of the answer across 'one choice' is a coincidence of the surface, since the setter's mechanism uses 'that's not on ice'
taken as written into the letter pool

explanation.surface: A water spirit offered a single option that doesn't involve skating.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool the letters of ONE and CHOICE, take out the letters of ON ICE, and rearrange the four left over.
explanation.definitionFit: Echo was the mountain nymph in Greek myth who pined away for Narcissus until only her voice remained.

clue.text: Mel Gibson's lead becomes paltry part in "The Crucible"

indicators.note: the letter becomes part of the next word by being placed inside it

parts.note: tinpot means cheap and inferior, so paltry

indicators.note: a word's lead is its first letter

explanation.surface: Mel Gibson's star turn is reduced to a bit part in Arthur Miller's play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Crucible' looks like Arthur Miller's play about the Salem witch trials; here it is the vessel for melting metals. 'becomes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A crucible is a vessel in which metals are melted, which is literally what a melting pot is.

clue.text: Swan boxes match in colour

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
to agree is to match or correspond

explanation.surface: A swan wrapping up a matching colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Pea green is a shade of colour, the bright yellowish green of fresh peas.

clue.text: Solve 3 by 10 without editor getting to play a mean trick

parts.note: to do a puzzle is to solve it

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: three multiplied by ten makes thirty

explanation.surface: An instruction to solve a puzzle clue without help, leading to a dirty trick.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' and '10' look like cross-references to other clues, but they are plain numbers to multiply.
explanation.definitionFit: To do the dirty on someone is a British idiom meaning to treat them unfairly or deceitfully.

clue.text: I lit out to weaken argument

indicators.note: out means the letters of the words before it are taken away from the longer word

parts.note: to debilitate is to weaken

explanation.surface: Someone lights a fire to undermine a case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes the run ILIT (from 'I lit') from DEBILITATE, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A debate is a formal argument or discussion between opposing sides.

clue.text: Avidly ask for naughty fairy tales that educate?

parts.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite
lore is traditional knowledge passed down in stories

explanation.surface: Begging eagerly for wicked fairy stories with a moral.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore is to beg earnestly, which is asking for something avidly.

clue.text: Member that's horizontal managed to split the best part up

indicators.note: the word placed inside splits the other in two
in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: the most is the greatest part of something
to run something is to manage it, so ran is managed

explanation.surface: A level-headed club member contrived to break up the club's best bit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' looks like a club member; in building it means a structural part.
explanation.definitionFit: A transom is a horizontal crossbar in a window or over a door, a structural member.

clue.text: Overcoats with fleecing

indicators.note: over signals turning the word round, as if flipped head over heels

parts.note: macs are raincoats, short for mackintoshes

explanation.surface: Overcoats lined with wool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overcoats' is one word in the surface but splits into 'Over' (the reversal signal) and 'coats'. 'Fleecing' looks like a coat lining; it means swindling.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleecing is cheating someone out of money, and a scam is a swindle of that kind.

clue.text: Charlemagne then embraces one that's attractive

indicators.note: the words embrace, or hold within them, the letters we need

explanation.surface: The emperor Charlemagne hugs a charming companion.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnet attracts iron, and by extension a magnet is anyone or anything that draws people in.

clue.text: 17 girdled calendar girls to put a top on

indicators.note: to girdle is to encircle, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: 17-down means to beg, so this gives a synonym
the Calendar Girls were members of the Women's Institute, abbreviated WI

explanation.surface: Begging calendar models to put something on top.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute (WI) is a British women's organisation; its members posed for the famous Calendar Girls charity calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewig someone is to put a wig on their head, a wig being a kind of top covering.

clue.text: Any plight isn't right one to be trifled with

indicators.note: letters that aren't right are in the wrong order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Any trouble that's wrong should be taken lightly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaything is a toy, something or someone to be toyed or trifled with.

clue.text: Discipline of toddler when two?

indicators.note: a toddler's speech often turns an R into a W, so the word is said as a small child would

parts.note: to train is to discipline or school

explanation.surface: Asking whether a toddler's discipline starts at age two.
explanation.walkthrough: Toddlers often say W for R, so TRAIN becomes TWAIN, an old word for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Twain is an archaic word for two, as in 'never the twain shall meet'.

clue.text: Code protecting interior switches in explosive device

indicators.note: switches means the run of letters is turned to face the other way
the letters we need lie in the interior of these words

explanation.surface: A secret code guarding the inside changes within a bomb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interior' picks ODEPROT out of 'Code protecting', and 'switches' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: A torpedo is a self-propelled underwater missile, an explosive device fired at ships.

clue.text: Fuss about a league with ill-matched sides

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the others

parts.note: to make a scene is to make a fuss

explanation.surface: A row over a sports league where the teams are unevenly matched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ill-matched sides' suggests mismatched teams; it describes a triangle.
explanation.definitionFit: A scalene triangle has three sides all of different lengths.

clue.text: An increase in risk

parts.note: reads as a rise in danger, but means extra pay given for doing hazardous work

explanation.definitionFit: Danger money is a bonus payment made to workers for taking on hazardous duties.
